questions.stem: A 3-month-old baby was brought to the emergency department by her parents because of lethargy and irritability. She has not been eating well and has not had a bowel movement in several days. On examination, the infant has a depressed fontanel and notably poor muscle tone and a weak sucking reflex.
questions.lead_in: How does the cause of this illness appear under Gram stain?

options.text: Gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains

questions.explanation: Gram-positive bacilli Clostridium botulinum is an anaerobic, gram-positive bacillus. This patient has infant botulism caused by toxin production from this organism.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q37

questions.question: 3. 2 months old, admitted for constipation and poor feeding. In hospital, he evolves toward a clinical picture of dysphagia and symmetrical descending paralysis. He eventually requires intubation.

parts.text: What is the most probable diagnosis?
b) What sample and what test would you collect/order for him?
c) Apart from supportive measures, what are the most important aspect(s) of treatment of this condition?

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Infant botulism. Sample: Serum, stool. Test: Toxin neutralization bioassay in mice to detect botulinum toxin in serum, stool, enema fluid, gastric aspirate, or suspect foods, OR enriched selective media to isolate from stool/foods. Treatment: Human derived antitoxin (Human Botulism Immune Globulin) - significantly decreases days of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and total hospital stay by almost 1 month. Avoid aminoglycosides - will worsen paralysis. Equine derived heptavalent botulinum antitoxin for adult/peds botulism. Caution: delay routine live-virus vaccines for 6 months after receipt of BabyBIG.

questions.question: Dx test: toxin neutralizing bioassay to detect toxin in serum, stool, gastric asp, suspected foods.

parts.text: Dx test: toxin neutralizing bioassay to detect toxin in serum, stool, gastric asp, suspected foods.

questions.model_answer: Mouse toxin neutralization bioassay: serum, stool, gastric aspirate, and suspected food specimens are injected into mice pre-treated with type-specific antitoxin (and untreated controls); development of paralysis/death in unprotected mice but survival in antitoxin-protected mice confirms presence and type of botulinum toxin - remains the gold-standard confirmatory diagnostic test for botulism.

questions.question: In infants: botulinum toxin or botulinum toxin producing organisms in feces or toxin in serum.

parts.text: In infants: botulinum toxin or botulinum toxin producing organisms in feces or toxin in serum.

questions.model_answer: Infant botulism diagnosis: demonstration of botulinum toxin, or Clostridium botulinum organisms/spores, in the infant's stool (fecal culture/toxin assay) - stool is far more sensitive than serum in infants because toxin is produced in situ by organisms colonizing the infant gut (unlike foodborne botulism where preformed toxin is ingested); serum toxin detection is less reliably positive in infant botulism.

questions.question: 1mo with constipation, poor feeding, descending paralysis, loses gag reflex.

parts.text: Diagnosis
What specimen and test do you send to confirm diagnosis? (1mark)
What do you give this patient?
Other than infantile, what are three types of infection?
What is the specific therapy for management?

cohort_answer.text:
C botulinum: toxin acts in the cholinergic synapse. Foodborne botulism; Wound botulism; Inhalation botulism; Gastrointestinal (like infantile but for adults, colonized/infected by toxin-producing clostridia in those with loss of bowel flora)
Antitoxin (main treatment, ASAP after diagnosis). If wound botulism, consider penicillin after antitoxin (Pen G 3mu q4h, or flagyl 500 IV q8h as alternative). Avoid aminoglycosides, tetracycline, polymyxins - potentiate neuromuscular blockade

questions.question: You suspect your patient has botulism.

parts.text: a) What is the gold standard test for botulism?
b) What are four clinical specimens that can be sent for testing for botulism?

cohort_answer.text: Gold standard: mouse botulism bioassay/mouse lethality assay (patient samples injected intraperitoneally into mouse, toxin type determined by neutralization with specific antitoxins). Specimens: Foodborne - stool, vomitus, gastric fluid, suspected food sources; Infant - feces, serum, suspected foods, environmental samples; Wound - tissue, pus, serum (less sensitive).

questions.question: Botulism.

parts.text: What are 3 ways of acquiring excluding infant botulism. What is adjunctive specific therapy? In what one situation do you use additional specific therapy and what is it?

questions.model_answer: a) Three ways of acquiring botulism (excluding infant botulism): (1) Foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin in improperly canned/preserved food). (2) Wound botulism (toxin produced by C. botulinum contaminating a wound, classically associated with injection drug use/black tar heroin). (3) Iatrogenic (from cosmetic or therapeutic botulinum toxin injection, rare). b) Adjunctive specific therapy: heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT), equine-derived, given as early as possible in suspected foodborne/wound/adult botulism to neutralize circulating unbound toxin. c) Situation for additional specific therapy: infant botulism (<1 year old) - use human-derived Botulism Immune Globulin Intravenous (BabyBIG) instead of equine antitoxin, ideally within the first 3 days of hospitalization, given superior efficacy and avoidance of equine serum sensitization risk in infants.

parts.text: A) What are 3 ways of acquiring infant botulism?

cohort_answer.text: Infant botulism – ingestion of spores that germinate in infant's intestines and produce toxin, from home-canned vegetables, fruits, fish, honey. Foodborne botulism – preformed toxin ingested with food, absorbed in small intestine, reaches peripheral cholinergic synapses. Wound botulism – spores introduced into a wound where they germinate and produce toxin. Inhalational botulism – toxin absorbed through alveolar epithelium into bloodstream (speaker notes: contaminated food e.g. honey)

parts.text: B) What is adjunctive specific tx?

cohort_answer.text: If >1 year of age: HBAT (heptavalent botulinum antitoxin) - contains equine-derived antibody to 7 known botulinum toxin types, not approved for <1 year due to serious adverse effects and lifelong sensitization to equine proteins. If <1 year of age: BabyBIG (human botulinum immune globulin) 50mg/kg IV

parts.text: C) In what situation do you use additional specific therapy and what is it?

cohort_answer.text: Patients with wound botulism should undergo debridement even if the wound appears to be healing well. PenG 10-20 million units daily is recommended (alternative: metronidazole)

questions.question:
Q29 (2007)
Man with constipation, dysarthria, dysphagia

parts.text: A) Diagnosis?

cohort_answer.text: Botulism. Classic presentation: acute bilateral cranial neuropathies with symmetrical descending weakness. CDC cardinal features: fever absent (unless complicating infection), symmetrical neurologic manifestations, patient remains responsive, heart rate normal/slow absent hypotension, no sensory deficits except blurred vision

questions.question:
Q29 (2007)
Man with constipation, dysarthria, dysphagia

parts.text: B) 2 confirmatory tests

cohort_answer.text: Mouse bioassay; ELISA to detect botulinum toxin. [Background: conventional diagnosis relies on demonstration of toxin in serum, gastric secretions, stool, or food; mouse bioassay historically most sensitive]

questions.question: 2 month old baby presenting with weak cry, constipation, symmetrical descending flaccid paralysis

parts.text: A) Most likely dx
B) Method to confirm the dx?
C) 2 management strategies other than supportive care?
D) Pathogenesis

cohort_answer.text:
Botulism (typically <6 months, descending paralysis preceded by constipation). Ddx: acute flaccid paralysis from poliovirus, enterovirus, WNV, GBS, rabies
Botulinum toxin neutralization bioassay in mice; isolate toxin from serum/stool(highest yield)/enema fluid/gastric aspirate/suspect foods (often negative in infant); isolation of spores in food; EMG (non-specific)
BabyBIG (reduces ICU LOS, ventilation, hospitalization days); avoid antimicrobials (risk of lysis of intraluminal C. botulinum increasing toxin absorption, AG can potentiate neurotoxin)
Absorption of botulinum toxin into circulation from mucosa (toxin A and B important). Results from ingested spores which germinate/multiply/produce toxin in large gut via colonization. Neurotoxin blocks cholinergic neuromuscular innervation by preventing neurotransmitter release

questions.question: Man gardening, sustains a wound to his hand. Days/weeks later, seen in ER for pharyngitis, discharged home. Now progressive dysphagia and respiratory failure, has to be intubated and ventilated.

parts.text: Diagnosis

cohort_answer.text: Botulism. DDx: bacterial toxins (botulism, tetanus, gas gangrene, cutaneous anthrax); bacterial infections (regular SSTI, nocardia, mycobacteria, actinomycetoma, melioidosis); fungal (mycetoma - eumycetoma, sporothrix, dimorphic fungi, chromoblastomycosis, lobomycosis); parasitic (ectoparasites)

parts.text: Gold standard test
4 specimens to send for
Other than infantile, three other routes of infection
Specific therapy

cohort_answer.text: Gold standard: Mouse bioassay - neurotoxin detection. Specimens: Serum; Stool; gastric fluid; Wound (debrided tissue or anaerobic culture); Food suspected as source. Other routes: Wounds; Foodborne; Iatrogenic - cosmetic. Specific therapy: Botulinum antitoxin (BAT); Human derived botulism immune globulin - for infant botulism
